issues.item: Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help
issues.explanation: 'Avoid Medical Care' is internally inconsistent as written: the label indicates avoidance, but the item text states 'Seeking medical or psychological help,' which is the opposite behavior.

issues.item: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
issues.explanation: 'Overwork' is hard to reconcile with the patient's unemployment status. While unemployed people can keep excessively busy, this wording specifically implies excessive work as a strategy and is therefore clinically implausible for this demographic unless otherwise qualified.

issues.item: Overwork: work excessively to avoid being alone with thoughts
issues.explanation: These two items imply an active work-based avoidance pattern, which is hard to reconcile with the patient's stated occupation of unemployed. While keeping busy is plausible, 'Overwork' specifically describes excessive working and is therefore clinically incoherent with being unemployed unless supported by another role context that is not present here.

issues.item: Threat: Checking Behind: I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
issues.explanation: Checking whether someone is following her suggests a stalking/pursuit-type threat context that is not well aligned with the indexed trauma of physical abuse by a romantic partner, where fear is more typically focused on the partner in domestic spaces rather than unknown followers. With the rest of the profile centered on sleeping alone, vulnerability, restricted safe places, and sleep vigilance, this item pulls toward a different threat pattern.

issues.item: Memory: Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
issues.explanation: Bodily reenactment can occur in PTSD, but as selected here it implies a highly embodied, posture-specific trauma memory. Given the other memory items emphasize involuntary intrusion plus active truncation of recall, and the threat profile is oriented toward vigilance and restricted safety rather than reliving a specific assault configuration, this item is less well integrated with the rest of the formulation and self-report pattern.

vignette:
Amina is a 68-year-old African American woman who came to treatment after years of living carefully around fear she rarely named directly. She has been married for many years, but the trauma she described came from an earlier romantic relationship in which she was physically abused by a partner. When she speaks about that period, the scenes do not come in a calm, ordered story. They arrive suddenly, in pieces that feel immediate. She can begin to describe one night and then stop herself abruptly, her face tightening, as if she has reached a point past which it is dangerous to go. She says the memory "comes in by itself," and when it does, it is not like remembering something old. It is as if she is back there before she has any chance to prepare.

The incident she returns to most often happened at night after an argument had turned unpredictable. What stands out in her account is not only his violence but the helpless exposure of it: being alone with him, feeling emotionally open and unprotected, and becoming aware of the smell of earth from outside as part of the scene. She remembers the ground smell vividly, the damp outdoor odor coming in from outside the home and clinging to the moment. That sensory detail now carries unusual force. Even now, if she catches the smell of soil after rain or walks past freshly turned dirt, the whole scene can surge back without warning. She does not experience it as a thought she chooses to revisit. It feels imposed on her, instantaneous and complete.

In the months and years afterward, Amina shaped her life around not feeling exposed. Sleeping became one of the clearest places this showed up. She dreads sleeping alone and becomes especially distressed if she is in an unfamiliar place overnight. At those times she feels too unprotected to settle, as if sleep would mean dropping her guard when she cannot afford to. She lies awake listening, staying alert long past the point of exhaustion. Even in her own home she does not fully relax. She notices sounds, tracks where people are in the house, and remains watchful in a place she wishes she could simply inhabit. She described having only a very small number of places where her body feels convinced she is safe, and outside those spaces she feels herself tense and brace.

Her daily habits have gradually organized around reducing that sense of vulnerability. She keeps herself busy almost constantly. Although she is unemployed, her days are full by design: chores extended, errands multiplied, television or radio kept on, small tasks found and refound. If there is quiet, she feels her mind opening in ways that do not feel safe. She works hard to keep her attention occupied, shifting quickly to something else whenever she senses the memory approaching. When fragments begin to surface, she pushes them away before they can fully form. She knows this happens; she can feel herself stopping the recollection midstream. At the same time, she cannot stop the moments when it breaks through anyway.

In relationships, especially when she senses tension or emotional exposure, Amina tends to go along with what other people want. She describes this not as generosity but as a way to stay safe. It feels less risky to accommodate, to smooth things over, to avoid anything that might bring conflict close. Over time this has narrowed her life. She limits where she goes and feels most at ease only in a few familiar places. Even at home, where she spends much of her time, she is often scanning internally and externally rather than resting. Her husband sees how difficult nights are for her, especially if he is away or if she has to sleep in a setting that is not her own. Those nights can become nearly sleepless, with Amina remaining alert to the point of dawn.

What finally brought her to seek help was not one new event but the wearing accumulation of this way of living. She had become tired of arranging every day around staying occupied and every night around staying watchful. Recently, after encountering the smell of fresh soil outdoors, she was hit by the memory so suddenly that it left her shaken for hours, and she realized how little control she felt she had over when the past entered the present. She came to treatment wanting, above all, to feel less trapped by these sudden returns of memory and less confined to the few places where she can breathe easily. What frightens her most is the sense that vulnerability can appear anywhere, without warning; what she hopes for is to be able to rest, especially at night, without feeling she must remain on guard.
